title: What have we learned from the new Viking ship?

paragraphs.text: A bold archaeological experiment involving a 1,200-mile voyage from Scandinavia to Ireland is transforming the academic world's understanding of Viking* seafaring. Compared to what we know about Roman and Greek seafaring, modern scholars know little about just how the Vikings achieved their extraordinary maritime successes. In an attempt to learn more, a group of 21st-century 'Vikings'-in the form of Danish archaeologists and historians-built and sailed a life-sized copy or replica Viking warship called the Sea Stallion.

The remains of the original vessel were discovered and recovered by archaeologists in Denmark half a century ago. Research revealed it had been built in the Irish city of Dublin in 1042 and deliberately sunk in Denmark three decades later. The 30-metre-long replica of the ship built to the specifications of the original vessel arrived in Ireland after an adventure lasting six and a half weeks. Although the experiment on the high seas was fraught with danger (at one stage the vessel almost sank), preliminary results suggest that the voyage really has begun to solve some of the greatest riddles of the Viking Age.

The ship's design The experiment using the replica ship has revealed that Viking longships were much more complex, in terms of structure, than previously thought. When the replica vessel was put through the initial sea trials, the entire hull bent back and forth from port to starboard by as much as 60 centimetres as it cut through the waves. The ship was so flexible that key Viking-style wooden nails began to work loose, and the entire structure was in danger of falling apart. After more detailed examination of the archaeological remains of the original vessel, the archaeologists realised that the Vikings had incorporated substantial strengthening timbers into the structure to give the vessel greater rigidity.

As a trial, an additional large longitudinal timber was added to the replica and deck planks were fastened to the vessel's cross beams. This more sophisticated design was tested in the 1,200-mile voyage and, by all accounts, worked well.

Sailing the replica ship Archaeologists on the project carried out by Denmark's Viking Ship Museum think the really big Viking warships were 20 per cent slower than had been assumed. The experimental voyage has revealed that, although theoretically the warships could go extremely fast, their speed was limited by the strength of one small piece of kit-the fastening mechanism used in the steering system. Viking ships used side rudders, but as the vessel cut through the waves, these rudders came under massive pressure. As a result, the rope that fastened the rudders to the hull would have broken if the vessel travelled faster than 16 knots. The experimental voyage has revealed how the fastener was the major limiting factor on the speed-and therefore, to a degree, on the range-of large Viking warships.

The vital importance of guaranteeing the integrity of this rudder fastener was demonstrated with terrifying clarity during the voyage when, during a storm in the Irish sea, it broke, causing the ship to lurch out of control. Instead of sailing smoothly through the alarming six-metre waves, the longship turned through 90 degrees so that the waves were buffeting its sides, putting the ship in danger of being swamped. Amid the acute danger, the rope was replaced but the incident could have sunk the vessel.

The experiment also suggests that the technology used to control the rigging-the so-called needles employed to tighten the key ropes-was probably more sophisticated than previously thought. The needles used on the experimental voyage kept breaking, so archaeologists had to test other designs for clues as to what the Vikings originally used.

Living conditions on board ship Like its 11th-century predecessor, the modern-day vessel is 30 metres long. Each of the 61 crew members has 1.5 square metres of what could euphemistically be called personal space. The linen (flax) sail measures 10 by 11.2 metres and weighs 200 kilogrammes. The 60 oars each weigh in at 9.5 kilogrammes and are 4.3 metres in length.

The experimental voyage also suggests the original Vikings probably had rudimentary tents (made of woollen cloth and smeared with foul smelling fat and tar) on board. Until now, academics have been divided on this issue: linguistic ambiguity in the ancient Viking sagas has led some scholars to conclude that Viking seamen braved wind and rain without the need for shelter, while others argue the opposite. This experimental voyage demonstrated that, in the closely packed environment of a Viking ship, it is impossible to get proper rest in the elements without shelter. Had Viking sailors not slept properly, they would simply not have been fighting fit at the end of their voyage.

More for sailing than rowing Until now, marine archaeologists and historians have regarded Viking longships as combined sailing and rowing vessels. Now, they have concluded that these vessels were in reality mainly sailing ships with relatively limited rowing capability. Rowing such vessels was more difficult than has been assumed, and the researchers now believe oars were mainly employed on rivers and fjords.

questions.prompt: The 21st-century 'Vikings' who carried out the experiment were professional sailors.
The 11th-century Viking ship on which the replica ship was based was found in Dublin.
The original ship was in poor condition when it was sunk.
The arrival of the replica ship in Ireland received considerable media coverage.
During the sea trials of the replica ship, its flexibility proved a valuable asset.
Only wooden nails were available in Viking times.
For its voyage, extra wooden boards were used to strengthen the replica ship.

questions.prompt: How much slower do the project archaeologists think the large Viking warships were than had been previously thought?
On Viking ships, what were the rudder fastening mechanisms made of?
What were used to keep the rigging tight on Viking ships?
How much individual room is each of the replica ship's crew members allowed?
What did having a shelter on board allow the Viking sailors to have?
What TWO types of waterways do marine experts now think that Viking ships were rowed on?
